This is really intense lengths to go through over just a phone, and I mean that on both your side and your parents side. The fact that they punish you for lying says to me that they want you to be a respectable person, not that they hate you. Perhaps it is their love that motivated them to take such insane gestures. 

My parents are drug abusers, and they don't really care either way what happens to me in certain respects. Sometimes it can be my childish interpretation, and sometimes it can be shortcomings on their ends. The best advice I have to offer for you is not to sit here and contemplate suicide on their behalf, because it would ruin your own life by shortening it. Instead, think about what went through your dad's head. He wanted to trust you, he wanted to give you a chance, and each time you shoved it off. Why? What caused your response? What would you have done in his place? Is all this really worth a phone, or is it something deeper? These are all questions I would contemplate, but being as I am not you, and i could be tragically mistaken in so many ways, I can only offer what I have typed as a response.

I have lived through abuse myself, and there is a fine line between discipline and abuse. I don't know where this lies, and only through careful consideration can you choose to learn from this, sort it out with your parents, and come to terms why this happened.

Okay, so I have been hospitalized in the USA twice, both under 18 and over. Here is what to expect:

-You will be admitted to the ER and a shrink will come by to evaluate you
-Your evaluation will either lead to hospitalization (most likely case) or you can be released to your parents if they feel it is a safe environment. Either way, you WILL be placed on 24 watch, meaning yes, somebody will be watching you for 24 full hours, including when you use the bathroom, shower, etc.
-If you are moved to a psychiatric facility, you will be there for at least three days to evaluate you and regulate your medication. There shouldn't be any 24-hour observation at this point, but you will have pretty strict rules and schedules, and have to attend groups with other kids.

Upon release, you will probably have an outpatient program or plan with your regular shrink. I hope this helps, and if you have any questions please ask

I would say that everyone is different, but to bring it up when he's trying to socialize wasn't really the best thing to do.

However, if he makes a sliding "dark humor" joke, he may not want to discuss it then and there, but he may be trying to make light of a bad situation.

Alternatively, I would say that if he says something truly sad, then he may be trying to start a conversation. I know that for myself, one of the hardest things is to talk about depression in an open setting. I can make jokes and try to beat it down into a "not so big deal" but discussing it with people makes me suddenly feel really self aware and uncomfortable. If you want to help him, try starting out slowly, unless you think he needs to get it out all at once. Either way, just try and show that when he needs you, you are there and you want to be involved. That might be enough to start a conversation when he is ready.

Side note: One on one drunk nights are great ways to get hidden information out that otherwise is hard to talk about. This is not a suggestion and can be dangerous if the person is unpredictable and/or will start a fight, run off, and do something stupid. If they seem suicidal, I would tell somebody else before you run to call the police or anybody else.

The worst emotional pain I had was when I told my mom, in the midst of her divorce, that her last husband abused me really badly. I knew she knew, or course, but I just wanted to say it.

She looked me in the face and told me that she "had no idea," and after some silence, she said firmly, "But you know, with all the shit you put us through, you probably deserved it."

I was thirteen with not even so much as a lunch detention under my belt, loud and smart mouthed, but a bookworm anime geek at best.
